headline: Linear KV cache scaling does not imply memory is the only bottleneck or that memory savings yield proportional speedup
claim: Linear KV cache scaling with sequence length and batch size does not imply memory is the only bottleneck or that memory savings yield proportional speedup.
paper_fact: scaling linearly with the sequence length and batch size.
premise: Amdahl's law and memory-hierarchy effects mean reducing one resource need not yield proportional end-to-end speedup; bottlenecks can shift.
inference: The paper's linear-scaling observation and memory savings are necessary but not sufficient for proportional throughput or latency gains; net benefit depends on batch, offload, hardware, and eviction overhead.
toy_example: Toy example, not a measurement: a cache that shrinks from 100 to 20 entries but spends 10 units per step scoring evictions may save memory yet not improve tokens/s if compute-bound.
conditional_consequence: If the workload is compute-bound or eviction scoring overhead dominates, memory savings may not translate into proportional throughput or latency improvement.
critical_link: The link is the system's ability to convert freed memory into larger batch or avoided offload without adding compute or I/O overhead.
necessary_conditions: Workload is memory-bound rather than compute-bound
Freed memory can be converted into larger batch or less offload
Eviction scoring overhead does not dominate
Hardware and system support the larger batch
defeaters: Paper reports up to 29×, 29×, and 3× throughput improvements
Paper reports up to 1.9× latency reduction
Paper includes prefill, generation, and cache construction time in speedups
do_not_infer: Do not infer linear KV scaling implies linear speedup
Do not infer memory is the only bottleneck
Do not infer authors claim proportional speedup from memory reduction
author_boundaries: Authors report measured speedups for H2O in tested systems; they do not claim memory savings alone guarantee proportional speedup.
lens: L6: cost shifts to eviction and score computation

quotes.text: scaling linearly with the sequence length and batch size.
the memory usage is reduced, which brings two advantages: 1) we can use a much larger batch size; 2) we can make a setting from requiring offloading to not requiring offloading.
With the same batch size, H2O can reduce the latency by up to 1.9×.

mechanism: Amdahl's law and memory-hierarchy effects mean reducing one resource need not yield proportional end-to-end speedup; bottlenecks can shift. The paper's linear-scaling observation and memory savings are necessary but not sufficient for proportional throughput or latency gains; net benefit depends on batch, offload, hardware, and eviction overhead.

headline: A low-cost greedy eviction policy does not imply or guarantee net throughput improvement.
claim: The per-step argmax over k candidates can add score-computation and cache-replacement cost that offsets memory savings; end-to-end benefit is not guaranteed by the policy being called low-cost.
paper_fact: we present a greedy but low-cost variant of H2 which is dynamically determined by the accumulated attention score at each decoding step
premise: Argmax over k candidates per token per head/layer costs O(k) score evaluations; memory savings only improve throughput when memory bandwidth or capacity is the bottleneck.
inference: The paper's throughput results are end-to-end and include cache construction, but they do not isolate the eviction-score cost, so net benefit depends on k, batch, hardware, and implementation.
toy_example: Not a measurement: with k=4096, scanning all candidates per head per layer could cost more than the memory saved, but this is not measured here.
conditional_consequence: If k is large or score computation is expensive, then per-step argmax cost may offset memory savings; the paper does not isolate this cost.
critical_link: No per-step cost breakdown is shown; 'low-cost' is relative to alternatives, not a guarantee that eviction overhead is negligible.
necessary_conditions: k is small enough that O(k) scoring is cheap
memory capacity/bandwidth is the dominant bottleneck
cache replacement is cheap relative to attention
batch size is large enough to amortize overhead
defeaters: Measured throughput improvement with isolated eviction cost negligible
k is small in all reported settings
Score computation is fused and free in implementation
do_not_infer: Do not infer H2O has no speedup
Do not infer eviction cost exceeds savings
Do not infer the paper failed to measure throughput

quotes.text: we present a greedy but low-cost variant of H2 which is dynamically determined by the accumulated attention score at each decoding step
All the speedup results are tested in an end-to-end setting, including both the pre-filling and generation phases. And it includes the time for constructing the H2O KV cache.

author_boundaries: Authors report end-to-end throughput including cache construction; they do not isolate per-step eviction cost.
inferred_consequence: Net throughput benefit depends on unisolated eviction overhead and workload parameters; it is not guaranteed by the policy's low-cost label.
mechanism: Argmax over k candidates per token per head/layer costs O(k) score evaluations; memory savings only improve throughput when memory bandwidth or capacity is the bottleneck. The paper's throughput results are end-to-end and include cache construction, but they do not isolate the eviction-score cost, so net benefit depends on k, batch, hardware, and implementation.

headline: A fixed KV cache budget does not imply a target accuracy or latency
claim: A fixed KV cache budget k does not imply a target accuracy or latency; the eviction policy, workload, and system overhead determine outcomes.
paper_fact: Our goal is to find a KV cache eviction policy such that the output of the generative process is similar or comparable to the original one without limiting the cache size.
premise: A cache budget is a capacity constraint; accuracy depends on which entries are kept and the task, while latency depends on compute, I/O, and eviction overhead.
inference: The paper's 20% budget results and speedups are empirical for H2O and tested settings; they do not make k an accuracy or latency target.
toy_example: Toy example, not a measurement: two eviction policies with the same k can retain different tokens and produce different accuracy.
conditional_consequence: If eviction overhead grows with k or the task needs long-context information, a given k may not deliver the reported accuracy or speed.
critical_link: The link is the mapping from budget k to retained information and from system overhead to wall-clock time; k alone fixes neither.
necessary_conditions: Eviction policy selects tokens that preserve task-relevant information
System overhead of eviction is small relative to saved memory
Batch size or offload can be adjusted to exploit freed memory
defeaters: Paper reports 20% budget comparable on many tasks
Paper reports throughput and latency gains
Paper includes construction time in speedups
do_not_infer: Do not infer k is an accuracy target
Do not infer same k yields same accuracy across policies
Do not infer authors claim budget alone determines latency
author_boundaries: Authors report empirical results for H2O at selected budgets; they do not claim k alone sets accuracy or latency.
lens: L2: budget is not an accuracy target

quotes.text: Let k denote the budget of space and k < n.
Our goal is to find a KV cache eviction policy such that the output of the generative process is similar or comparable to the original one without limiting the cache size.
With the same batch size, H2O can reduce the latency by up to 1.9×.

mechanism: A cache budget is a capacity constraint; accuracy depends on which entries are kept and the task, while latency depends on compute, I/O, and eviction overhead. The paper's 20% budget results and speedups are empirical for H2O and tested settings; they do not make k an accuracy or latency target.

headline: Per-step local greedy selection does not imply or guarantee globally optimal KV-cache eviction.
claim: The low-cost local greedy H2 policy is not a global optimizer; the paper's guarantee is conditional on submodularity and mild assumptions.
paper_fact: We formulate the KV cache eviction as a dynamic submodular problem and prove (under mild assumptions) a theoretical guarantee for our novel eviction algorithm
premise: Greedy per-step selection is not global optimization; approximation guarantees require assumptions such as submodularity.
inference: Without the stated assumptions or when future attention diverges from local scores, local greedy eviction has no general global-optimality guarantee.
conditional_consequence: If the attention scheme is not submodular or future importance diverges, local greedy selection may be suboptimal even if it is low-cost.
critical_link: The theorem's assumptions must hold for the guarantee to apply; empirical equal effectiveness is not a proof of global optimality.
necessary_conditions: The attention scheme satisfies the paper's submodularity or mild assumptions.
The approximation parameters remain within the theorem's bounds.
Local accumulated scores remain predictive of future importance.
defeaters: The paper reports empirical equal effectiveness of local and future-aware H2.
The paper provides a theoretical guarantee under mild assumptions.
H2O performs well across many reported benchmarks.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the paper claims global optimality without assumptions.
Do not infer that lack of a global guarantee means poor empirical performance.
Do not infer that greedy local selection is always suboptimal.

quotes.text: We formulate the KV cache eviction as a dynamic submodular problem and prove (under mild assumptions) a theoretical guarantee for our novel eviction algorithm
Assuming the attention scheme is submodular, then greedily constructing the set Si (without cache size limitation) satisfies the near-optimal property in terms of submodular.

author_boundaries: Authors state the guarantee is under mild assumptions.
Authors present the greedy policy as low-cost and empirically effective.
Authors do not claim unconditional global optimality.
inferred_consequences: The guarantee is conditional, not universal.
Deployment outside the assumed regime may lack the stated approximation bound.
mechanism: Greedy per-step selection is not global optimization; approximation guarantees require assumptions such as submodularity. Without the stated assumptions or when future attention diverges from local scores, local greedy eviction has no general global-optimality guarantee.

headline: Lower streaming perplexity with H2O does not imply or guarantee better performance on all long-context tasks.
claim: H2O plus StreamLLM's lower PG-19 perplexity at up to four million tokens is evidence of language-modeling fit, not a guarantee of downstream long-context QA, summarization, or retrieval success.
paper_fact: better performance (lower perplexity) than the original StreamLLM method
premise: Perplexity is a next-token likelihood metric on a text sample; it is not a task-specific accuracy metric.
inference: The reported lower PG-19 perplexity supports a language-modeling proxy for streaming, not a guarantee of downstream long-context task success.
conditional_consequence: If a downstream task requires retrieving a specific fact or summarizing dispersed content, then lower streaming perplexity alone cannot establish success; task-specific evaluation is needed.
critical_link: The paper's 4M-token claim is tied to streaming perplexity on the first PG-19 sample, while the mechanism's eviction policy can still drop task-critical tokens.
necessary_conditions: Task-specific long-context evaluation is performed.
The cache budget and H2 selection retain the information needed by the task.
Perplexity is not treated as a substitute for task accuracy.
defeaters: Paper reports H2O better on multi-document QA and summarization than StreamLLM.
If the downstream task is language modeling on similar text, perplexity may be directly relevant.
If H2O matches full-cache performance on the task, the concern is reduced.
do_not_infer: Do not infer H2O fails all long-context tasks.
Do not infer perplexity is irrelevant to language modeling.
Do not infer the 4M-token result is invalid.

quotes.text: better performance (lower perplexity) than the original StreamLLM method

H2O can empower LLMs to tackle input with length up to four mil-
lion tokens

author_boundaries: Authors claim 4M-token streaming and lower PG-19 perplexity than StreamLLM; they do not claim universal downstream long-context success.
Authors report H2O better on multi-document QA and summarization, but not an exhaustive all-task guarantee.
inferred_consequences: Task-specific long-context tests are needed before treating lower streaming perplexity as general long-context competence.
mechanism: Perplexity is a next-token likelihood metric on a text sample; it is not a task-specific accuracy metric. The reported lower PG-19 perplexity supports a language-modeling proxy for streaming, not a guarantee of downstream long-context task success.

headline: Lower Self-BLEU does not imply or guarantee increased creativity or quality
claim: H2O's reported lower Self-BLEU and qualitative examples do not establish increased creativity or quality; they support at most a slight diversity/repetition change in the reported setup.
paper_fact: The comparatively lower Self-BELU score of H2O indicates the slightly increased diversity of generated text.
premise: Self-BLEU is an n-gram overlap diversity proxy; lower values can indicate more diversity but can also reflect degeneration or off-topic output. Creativity and quality require human or task-specific evaluation.
inference: The paper's evidence supports a small Self-BLEU decrease on 100 XSUM prompts with LLaMA-7B and qualitative examples, not a general creativity or quality improvement.
conditional_consequence: If a deployment treats H2O as a creativity or quality booster, it may overclaim; if diversity is desired, validate with human and task-specific metrics.
critical_link: The link from Self-BLEU and qualitative repetition examples to creativity or quality is not established.
necessary_conditions: Human evaluation of creativity/quality
Task-specific quality and faithfulness metrics
Multiple prompts and models
Same decoding settings across compared methods
defeaters: Human evaluation showing improved creativity without quality loss
Task metrics showing no quality tradeoff across diverse tasks
do_not_infer: H2O guarantees creativity
Lower Self-BLEU always means better text
Qualitative examples are a measurement of quality

quotes.text: The comparatively lower Self-BELU score of H2O indicates the slightly increased diversity of generated text.
H2O can generate sentences with fewer repeated words and more creativity

author_boundaries: Authors report a bonus effect and qualitative examples; they do not provide a human creativity/quality evaluation or a general creativity guarantee.
inferred_consequence: The diversity bonus should be treated as a reported side effect, not as evidence of improved creativity or quality.
mechanism: Self-BLEU is an n-gram overlap diversity proxy; lower values can indicate more diversity but can also reflect degeneration or off-topic output. Creativity and quality require human or task-specific evaluation. The paper's evidence supports a small Self-BLEU decrease on 100 XSUM prompts with LLaMA-7B and qualitative examples, not a general creativity or quality improvement.

headline: A 20% KV cache budget with H2O does not imply or guarantee comparable accuracy across all inference regimes.
claim: The paper's 20% budget result is not universal; zero-shot and one-shot tasks may require a higher KV cache budget of 30-40%.
paper_fact: However, unlike 5-shot, we also found that some tasks are more difficult, and the model requires more information to generate the correct content, resulting in a higher KV cache budget (30-40%).
premise: The cache budget required for comparable accuracy depends on task difficulty, prompt length, and how much information must be retained.
inference: The reported 20% budget success is conditional on the evaluation regime and task, not a guarantee for all settings.
toy_example: Not a measurement: a short 0-shot prompt with a critical fact in the middle may need more than 20% cache to retain that fact.
conditional_consequence: If a task is evaluated in a 0/1-shot regime with short prompts and needs more information, a 20% budget may underperform and require 30-40% instead.
critical_link: The link is the paper's own 30-40% budget note for 0/1-shot tasks; without that, 20% could be misread as a universal budget.
necessary_conditions: Evaluation regime is zero-shot or one-shot with short prompts.
The task requires more information than a 20% cache can retain.
Comparable accuracy to the full-cache model is the target.
defeaters: Main 5-shot results show 20% comparable on many tasks.
The 30-40% note applies to some tasks, not all.
A higher budget may still be much less than full cache.
do_not_infer: Do not infer 20% never works.
Do not infer H2O fails on all short prompts.
Do not infer the paper's main claim is false.

quotes.text: However, unlike 5-shot, we also found that some tasks are more difficult, and the model requires more information to generate the correct content, resulting in a higher KV cache budget (30-40%).
(2) Meanwhile, with less than 20% KV cache budget(i.e., more than 5× memory reduction), H2O achieves comparable performance as the model with full KV embeddings;

mechanism: The cache budget required for comparable accuracy depends on task difficulty, prompt length, and how much information must be retained. The reported 20% budget success is conditional on the evaluation regime and task, not a guarantee for all settings.

headline: A dynamic submodular approximation guarantee does not imply or guarantee runtime throughput or memory savings.
claim: The theorem concerns a set-function value under assumptions, not wall-clock throughput, latency, or memory reduction; those are empirical system results.
paper_fact: We formulate the KV cache eviction as a dynamic submodular problem and prove (under mild assumptions) a theoretical guarantee for our novel eviction algorithm which could help guide future work.
premise: Theoretical approximation bounds are not measurements of wall-clock throughput, latency, or memory; system performance depends on implementation and hardware.
inference: The submodular theorem does not establish the reported throughput or memory reductions; those claims rest on the system experiments.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): an algorithm with a better f-bound but large per-token overhead could be slower in wall-clock time.
conditional_consequence: If implementation overhead or hardware differs, the theorem can hold while throughput gains shrink or vanish.
critical_link: Separation between the theorem's set-function objective and measured system metrics.
necessary_conditions: the theorem's assumptions hold
the implementation realizes the analyzed greedy eviction
throughput is measured under stated hardware, batch, and offload conditions
defeaters: direct end-to-end throughput/latency measurements
ablation isolating eviction overhead
the theorem is explicitly not claimed to prove system speedups
do_not_infer: do not infer the theorem proves no speedup
do not infer the reported speedups are invalid
do not infer theoretical guidance is useless

quotes.text: We formulate the KV cache eviction as a dynamic submodular problem and prove (under mild assumptions) a theoretical guarantee for our novel eviction algorithm which could help guide future work.
The analysis shows that it results in a similar generative process as the one using the H2 eviction policy.

author_boundaries: Authors present the theorem as theoretical guidance and report throughput from system experiments.
Authors do not claim the theorem itself proves throughput or memory savings.
inferred_consequences: The theorem and system speedup claims should be kept separate.
Throughput claims depend on benchmark conditions.
mechanism: Theoretical approximation bounds are not measurements of wall-clock throughput, latency, or memory; system performance depends on implementation and hardware. The submodular theorem does not establish the reported throughput or memory reductions; those claims rest on the system experiments.

headline: A 20% KV-cache budget does not guarantee comparable accuracy across all tasks and sequence lengths
claim: The 20% budget is an empirical main-result setting, not a universal accuracy guarantee; the paper reports some 0/1-shot tasks needing 30-40% and benchmarks long sequences for throughput/latency potential.
paper_fact: H2O with 20% heavy hitters improves the throughput over three leading inference systems DeepSpeed Zero-Inference, Hugging Face Accelerate, and FlexGen by up to 29×, 29×, and 3×
premise: Throughput and accuracy are distinct metrics; a budget fraction selected for throughput does not by itself establish accuracy parity.
inference: Therefore, the reported 20% throughput gains do not guarantee comparable accuracy for every task or sequence length; the paper's accuracy claims are limited to tested settings and some tasks need 30-40%.
conditional_consequence: If a task or sequence length is outside the tested distribution or is more difficult, then a fixed 20% budget may not preserve accuracy.
critical_link: The paper reports both throughput at 20% and comparable accuracy on many tasks, but also reports higher budget needs for 0/1-shot; a universal accuracy guarantee is not established.

Paper's comparable accuracy holds for the specific benchmark.
Longer sequence throughput tests are not accuracy tests.
Higher budget note is for 0/1-shot, not all tasks.
do_not_infer: Do not infer the paper claims universal accuracy at 20%.
Do not infer throughput speedups imply accuracy.
Do not infer 20% fails on all tasks.
Do not infer long-sequence throughput results are accuracy results.
Author boundary: the paper's 20% main results and 30-40% 0/1-shot note are separate empirical settings.

headline: A 20% KV-cache budget does not imply or guarantee throughput speedup proportional to the memory reduction.
claim: The reported 5–10× KV-cache memory reduction and up to 3×/29×/29× throughput gains are separate system measurements; one does not imply the other.
paper_fact: H2O with a 20% budget improves the generation throughput over FlexGen, DeepSpeed, and Accelerate by up to 3×, 29×, and 29×
premise: Throughput speedup is not a linear function of memory footprint; it depends on baseline efficiency, hardware, batch size, offload, and eviction overhead.
inference: The paper reports memory reduction and throughput gains as measured outcomes under specific baselines and hardware, not as a proportional law.
toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): halving cache size does not halve wall-clock if attention compute dominates.
conditional_consequence: If the baseline is already optimized or the workload is compute-bound, then throughput gain can be much smaller than the memory reduction.
critical_link: Memory savings must remove the actual bottleneck (KV capacity or offload) and not be offset by eviction or larger-batch compute.
necessary_conditions: memory-bound or offload-bound baseline
batch or offload limit is active
eviction overhead is included and acceptable
hardware and model match the reported regime
defeaters: compute-bound workload
baseline already fits and is optimized
high eviction overhead
different hardware or sequence length
do_not_infer: Do not infer that a 20% budget means 5× throughput.
Do not infer that 5–10× memory reduction means 5–10× speedup.

author_boundary: Authors report measured memory, throughput, and latency results on specified models and hardware; they do not claim proportional speedup from cache reduction.

headline: Accuracy parity on three OPT-30B tasks does not imply or guarantee general accuracy preservation.
claim: The reported H2O plus 4-bit accuracy parity is scoped to a narrow model-task setting and is not a general guarantee.
paper_fact: We use OPT-30B as our base model and COPA, OpenBookWA, and PiQA as evaluation tasks.
premise: A three-task, single-model accuracy check is a narrow compatibility test; quantization and eviction errors can vary by task, model, and cache budget.
inference: The reported parity supports compatibility for OPT-30B on those tasks, not a general guarantee across workloads.
conditional_consequence: If the model, task set, cache budget, or 4-bit kernel changes, H2O+4-bit may not preserve full-model accuracy.
critical_link: The paper does not report a broad sweep across models, tasks, and budgets for the 4-bit combination.

FlexGen 4-bit quantization
reported cache budget and settings
defeaters: A broad multi-model, multi-task sweep showing parity

Evidence that the three tasks are representative

headline: One XSUM/LLaMA-7B Self-BLEU result does not imply or guarantee general reduced repetition across models and tasks

paper_fact: We randomly sample 100 instances from the XSUM dataset, as prompts. Subsequently, we employed the LLaMa-7B to generate text of equal length.
premise: Diversity and repetition depend on model family, task, prompt length, decoding strategy, and cache budget; a single model/task/sample cannot establish a general effect.
inference: The paper's quantitative diversity evidence is a single XSUM/LLaMA-7B setup, and the qualitative examples are illustrative; generalization to other H2O deployments is not guaranteed.
conditional_consequence: For other models or tasks, H2O may not reduce repetition or increase diversity; users should evaluate the effect in their own setting before relying on it.
critical_link: Generalization from one Self-BLEU setup and qualitative examples to a general reduced-repetition bonus.

Statistical tests on diversity and repetition metrics
Consistent cache budgets and baselines
defeaters: Broad replication showing reduced repetition across models and tasks
